I came in because… honestly, it’s getting hard to explain things in a way people can follow. I’m an artist, so I’m used to being a little abstract, and sometimes my work does move between textures and color and meaning, but lately it’s like my thoughts are jumping too fast or too sideways.

Like, I’ll be writing an artist statement and I start with the surface of a piece, the materials, the texture, and then suddenly I’m talking about the budget, or what a client said, or some hidden meaning I feel is connected, and when I read it back it sort of makes sense to me in the moment, but other people say they can’t tell what I’m trying to say. It’s happening in client notes too, not just creative writing, which is embarrassing. And in meetings I’ll be explaining something and people look confused, or they’ll ask me to slow down or repeat myself, and then I realize I’ve skipped three steps and landed somewhere else completely.

So I guess I’m here because it’s starting to affect my work and how I come across. I don’t feel like I’m trying to be confusing, but what comes out doesn’t always line up in a normal order.

I’m not totally sure how to separate anxiety from just… embarrassment, I guess. I do feel self-conscious sometimes, especially in work settings, because once someone gets that confused look, I can feel myself trying to monitor every sentence while I’m still talking. And then that almost makes it harder, because I’m half explaining and half checking myself from the outside.

But I wouldn’t say I’m scared of people exactly, or that I’m avoiding everyone. It’s more like I get very aware of how I’m coming across. Like, am I making sense, did I skip something, are they being polite but lost, that kind of thing. I’ll sometimes over-explain because I’m trying to prevent the confusion, and then I worry I’ve made it worse by adding too much.

So… yes, self-conscious, definitely. Anxious maybe, but in a situational way, mostly when I know I need to be clear and there are consequences if I’m not.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Yeah… I have noticed that, actually. It’s not always in a simple way, like “I’m in a bad mood so I can’t explain myself.” Sometimes it feels almost the opposite at first.

There are stretches where I feel really lit up, like my mind is moving fast but in a good way, and every idea feels connected and important and honestly kind of brilliant. In those moments I feel almost unstoppable, like if people could just keep up with me, they’d see the whole thing the way I do. And when I’m trying to explain something then, I don’t necessarily feel confused inside — I feel like it’s all very clear, almost too clear, but then it comes out in this flood and other people don’t know where I’m going with it.

But then if someone interrupts me or says, “I don’t understand,” or even makes a small comment that I’d normally be able to take fine, I can get irritated really quickly. Like sharper than the situation deserves. A collaborator can ask one practical question, and suddenly I feel like they’re blocking the whole vision or doubting me, and I’ll snap or sound defensive. Then later I’ll think, okay, that reaction was much bigger than what they actually said.

So yes, I think when the explaining gets harder, my mood is often either really elevated, like everything is charged and exciting, or I’m much more irritable than I mean to be.

Yes, very much. That’s actually one of the things that makes it so hard to finish anything clearly.

Like if I’m trying to write a proposal, I’ll sit down with a pretty specific intention — explain the concept, outline the materials, make it readable — and then something tiny can pull me completely off course. The buzz of a light above me, or a shadow moving on the wall, or even just seeing one line in an old notebook can suddenly feel like it’s connected to the whole project in some important way. And then instead of writing the proposal, I’m chasing that connection.

It doesn’t always feel like “distraction” in the moment, which is part of the problem. It feels relevant. Like the light buzzing has a rhythm, and then I’m thinking about sound, and then sound becomes part of the installation, and then I’m digging through old notes because I remember one sentence I wrote months ago that suddenly seems essential. By the time I come back, I may have three new ideas, but the actual proposal is still half-written and kind of scattered.

So yes, I get sidetracked easily, but not always by something big. Sometimes it’s really small, almost stupidly small, and then my brain treats it like a doorway into a completely different room.

Yes, I do. It’s hard for me to stay with just one idea long enough to explain it cleanly, especially if I’m writing something like a proposal where I’m supposed to be organized and make a clear case.

I’ll start with one thought, like, okay, I need to describe the concept. Yes. That’s actually a big part of why I came in, because it’s started showing up in places where I really need to sound clear.

Like with my artist statements, I’ll sit down intending to explain one piece in a normal way — what it’s made of, what I’m trying to explore, maybe the budget or installation needs — and then the statement starts jumping around. I’ll go from talking about textures, like fabric or concrete or the way light hits something, straight into the cost of materials, and then somehow into what I think the piece is secretly pointing to or what a certain pattern “means.” And when I’m writing it, it doesn’t always feel random to me. It feels like there’s a thread connecting all of it. But when I read it back later, or when someone else reads it, it’s like… I can see how they’d be lost.

It happens in client notes too, which is embarrassing. I’ll mean to write something practical, like measurements or changes they asked for, and then I’ll notice I’ve written a whole paragraph about the feeling of the surface or some hidden significance I thought was there, and I didn’t actually answer the basic question.

And in meetings, people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain. I’ll think I’m being thorough, but apparently I’m jumping from one category to another too fast — textures, budget, meaning, logistics, then back to meaning — and I lose them. So yes, fragmented is a good word for it. It’s not that I have no thoughts. It’s more like there are too many pieces, and I can’t always put them in an order other people can understand.

And in meetings I’ll be explaining something and people look confused, or they’ll ask me to slow down or repeat myself, and then I realize I’ve skipped three steps and landed somewhere else completely.\n\nSo I guess I’m here because it’s starting to affect my work and how I come across. I don’t feel like I’m trying to be confusing, but what comes out doesn’t always line up in a normal order.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that this jumping between ideas happens to you in most conversations, or is it mainly when you're discussing your art or writing?\n\nPatient: It’s… more than just the art now. At first I thought it was only because artist statements are kind of strange anyway, you know, you’re already trying to translate texture and color and meaning into words, so it seemed normal that I’d drift around a bit. But it’s been happening in client notes too, and those are supposed to be straightforward.\n\nLike I’ll start describing a material choice or a surface treatment, and then somehow I’m suddenly talking about the budget, or what the client said last week, or this hidden meaning I feel like is tied to the piece, and I don’t always notice the jump until someone points it out. In meetings it happens out loud too. I’ll think I’m explaining something clearly, but people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to say, or they ask me to back up because I’ve skipped over the part that connects one idea to the next.\n\nSo I guess the answer is it’s not every single conversation, but it’s definitely not only my writing or only when I’m being “artistic.” It’s showing up in regular work conversations too, and that’s what’s been worrying me.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding that this difficulty with explaining your thoughts is affecting your relationships with clients or colleagues?\n\nPatient: Yes. I mean, I wish I could say it was just awkward or that people are being picky, but it’s actually affecting things now.\n\nI’ve missed paid deadlines because I’ll send notes or proposals that I thought were close to finished, and then the client comes back saying they don’t understand what I’m recommending or what the next step is. And then I have to rewrite it, but the rewriting takes longer because I’m trying to make it make sense, and by then the deadline has slipped. It’s embarrassing because these are not just casual ideas in a sketchbook — they’re things people are paying me for.\n\nIn meetings, collaborators have gotten visibly confused. Like I’ll be talking about an installation plan, and I think I’m being very clear because in my head all the pieces are connected, but someone will stop me and say, “Wait, are we talking about the materials, the budget, or the layout?” And I realize I’ve somehow braided all of that together without explaining the transitions.\n\nThe worst was that an exhibition got postponed because my notes and proposals basically stopped being usable enough. Not completely nonsense, but not solid enough for people to build from or schedule around. That felt really bad, because it wasn’t just me being misunderstood — it actually affected other people’s work and timing.\n\nDoctor: Are you feeling anxious or self-conscious about speaking with others due to your difficulty explaining your thoughts?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure how to separate anxiety from just… embarrassment, I guess. I do feel self-conscious sometimes, especially in work settings, because once someone gets that confused look, I can feel myself trying to monitor every sentence while I’m still talking. And then that almost makes it harder, because I’m half explaining and half checking myself from the outside.\n\nBut I wouldn’t say I’m scared of people exactly, or that I’m avoiding everyone. It’s more like I get very aware of how I’m coming across. Like, am I making sense, did I skip something, are they being polite but lost, that kind of thing. I’ll sometimes over-explain because I’m trying to prevent the confusion, and then I worry I’ve made it worse by adding too much.\n\nSo… yes, self-conscious, definitely. Anxious maybe, but in a situational way, mostly when I know I need to be clear and there are consequences if I’m not.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling more irritable, sad, or euphoric, when you're having trouble explaining your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I have noticed that, actually. It’s not always in a simple way, like “I’m in a bad mood so I can’t explain myself.” Sometimes it feels almost the opposite at first.\n\nThere are stretches where I feel really lit up, like my mind is moving fast but in a good way, and every idea feels connected and important and honestly kind of brilliant. In those moments I feel almost unstoppable, like if people could just keep up with me, they’d see the whole thing the way I do. And when I’m trying to explain something then, I don’t necessarily feel confused inside — I feel like it’s all very clear, almost too clear, but then it comes out in this flood and other people don’t know where I’m going with it.\n\nBut then if someone interrupts me or says, “I don’t understand,” or even makes a small comment that I’d normally be able to take fine, I can get irritated really quickly. Like sharper than the situation deserves. A collaborator can ask one practical question, and suddenly I feel like they’re blocking the whole vision or doubting me, and I’ll snap or sound defensive. Then later I’ll think, okay, that reaction was much bigger than what they actually said.\n\nSo yes, I think when the explaining gets harder, my mood is often either really elevated, like everything is charged and exciting, or I’m much more irritable than I mean to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself getting easily sidetracked by other thoughts or stimuli when you're trying to explain something?\n\nPatient: Yes, very much. That’s actually one of the things that makes it so hard to finish anything clearly.\n\nLike if I’m trying to write a proposal, I’ll sit down with a pretty specific intention — explain the concept, outline the materials, make it readable — and then something tiny can pull me completely off course. The buzz of a light above me, or a shadow moving on the wall, or even just seeing one line in an old notebook can suddenly feel like it’s connected to the whole project in some important way. And then instead of writing the proposal, I’m chasing that connection.\n\nIt doesn’t always feel like “distraction” in the moment, which is part of the problem. It feels relevant. Like the light buzzing has a rhythm, and then I’m thinking about sound, and then sound becomes part of the installation, and then I’m digging through old notes because I remember one sentence I wrote months ago that suddenly seems essential. By the time I come back, I may have three new ideas, but the actual proposal is still half-written and kind of scattered.\n\nSo yes, I get sidetracked easily, but not always by something big. Sometimes it’s really small, almost stupidly small, and then my brain treats it like a doorway into a completely different room.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to focus on one idea for an extended period when you're trying to explain something?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do. It’s hard for me to stay with just one idea long enough to explain it cleanly, especially if I’m writing something like a proposal where I’m supposed to be organized and make a clear case.\n\nI’ll start with one thought, like, okay, I need to describe the concept. But then the buzz of a light, or a shadow on the wall, or even one sentence in an old notebook can pull me completely sideways. And it’s not just that I’m bored or procrastinating, exactly. In the moment it feels like that thing is connected, like it matters, like it’s pointing me toward something I should follow. So I’ll go off into that, and then suddenly I’m not explaining the original idea anymore — I’m in a whole different line of thought.\n\nBy the time I come back, if I come back, the original idea feels kind of… interrupted. Like I still know it’s there, but I’ve lost the straight path through it. So yes, focusing on one idea for an extended period is difficult, because almost anything can become a doorway into something else.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find that your thoughts feel disorganized or fragmented when you're trying to express them to others?\n\nPatient: Yes. I don’t feel like I’m trying to be confusing, but what comes out doesn’t always line up in a normal order.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that this jumping between ideas happens to you in most conversations, or is it mainly when you're discussing your art or writing?\n\nPatient: It’s… more than just the art now. At first I thought it was only because artist statements are kind of strange anyway, you know, you’re already trying to translate texture and color and meaning into words, so it seemed normal that I’d drift around a bit. But it’s been happening in client notes too, and those are supposed to be straightforward.\n\nLike I’ll start describing a material choice or a surface treatment, and then somehow I’m suddenly talking about the budget, or what the client said last week, or this hidden meaning I feel like is tied to the piece, and I don’t always notice the jump until someone points it out. In meetings it happens out loud too. I’ll think I’m explaining something clearly, but people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to say, or they ask me to back up because I’ve skipped over the part that connects one idea to the next.\n\nSo I guess the answer is it’s not every single conversation, but it’s definitely not only my writing or only when I’m being “artistic.” It’s showing up in regular work conversations too, and that’s what’s been worrying me.\n\nDoctor: Are you finding that this difficulty with explaining your thoughts is affecting your relationships with clients or colleagues?\n\nPatient: Yes. I mean, I wish I could say it was just awkward or that people are being picky, but it’s actually affecting things now.\n\nI’ve missed paid deadlines because I’ll send notes or proposals that I thought were close to finished, and then the client comes back saying they don’t understand what I’m recommending or what the next step is. And then I have to rewrite it, but the rewriting takes longer because I’m trying to make it make sense, and by then the deadline has slipped. It’s embarrassing because these are not just casual ideas in a sketchbook — they’re things people are paying me for.\n\nIn meetings, collaborators have gotten visibly confused. Like I’ll be talking about an installation plan, and I think I’m being very clear because in my head all the pieces are connected, but someone will stop me and say, “Wait, are we talking about the materials, the budget, or the layout?” And I realize I’ve somehow braided all of that together without explaining the transitions.\n\nThe worst was that an exhibition got postponed because my notes and proposals basically stopped being usable enough. Not completely nonsense, but not solid enough for people to build from or schedule around. That felt really bad, because it wasn’t just me being misunderstood — it actually affected other people’s work and timing.\n\nDoctor: Are you feeling anxious or self-conscious about speaking with others due to your difficulty explaining your thoughts?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure how to separate anxiety from just… embarrassment, I guess. It’s more like I get very aware of how I’m coming across. Like, am I making sense, did I skip something, are they being polite but lost, that kind of thing. I’ll sometimes over-explain because I’m trying to prevent the confusion, and then I worry I’ve made it worse by adding too much.\n\nSo… yes, self-conscious, definitely. Anxious maybe, but in a situational way, mostly when I know I need to be clear and there are consequences if I’m not.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling more irritable, sad, or euphoric, when you're having trouble explaining your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I have noticed that, actually. In those moments I feel almost unstoppable, like if people could just keep up with me, they’d see the whole thing the way I do. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Yes, there are definitely days where it’s easier. I don’t want to make it sound like every sentence I say is impossible to follow, because that’s not true. If I’m just talking about groceries or a simple schedule thing, or if I’m answering something very direct, I can usually stay with it.

I’ll begin with textures, like the feel of a material or how something looks under light, and then suddenly I’m talking about budget, and then I’m explaining some secret meaning I feel like the piece has, and then I’m back to practical details again. In my head, while it’s happening, it feels connected, like I’m following a real line. But other people don’t seem to hear the line.

So, yes, there are clearer days. But when it’s not clear, it’s noticeable enough that people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain, and that’s embarrassing. It makes me second-guess whether I’m actually communicating or just sort of… piling thoughts on top of each other.

By the time I come back, I may have three new ideas, but the actual proposal is still half-written and kind of scattered.\n\nSo yes, I get sidetracked easily, but not always by something big. It’s hard for me to stay with just one idea long enough to explain it cleanly, especially if I’m writing something like a proposal where I’m supposed to be organized and make a clear case.\n\nI’ll start with one thought, like, okay, I need to describe the concept. In the moment it feels like that thing is connected, like it matters, like it’s pointing me toward something I should follow. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I think the biggest trigger is when I have to translate the work into words, if that makes sense. Like, I can be in the studio and the piece itself feels clear to me — the texture, the materials, the color, the way the surface catches light — but then the moment I have to write an artist statement or explain it to a client or talk about it in a meeting, it starts to get tangled.

It’s especially bad when there are practical things mixed in, like budget, deadlines, materials, or what the client wants. I’ll start by describing the texture or the visual idea, and then I’m suddenly talking about cost or logistics, and then I’ll jump into this deeper meaning I feel like the piece has, almost like there’s some hidden message in it, and then I’ll swing back to measurements or invoices or something very practical. In my head it feels like one connected explanation, but I can tell from people’s faces that it’s not landing that way.

So I don’t know if it’s one single event, exactly. It’s more like those situations where I’m expected to explain my art clearly — statements, client notes, meetings — seem to set it off or at least make it really obvious. That’s when people keep saying they can’t follow me, and that’s what made me feel like I needed to come in.

It’s more like I get very aware of how I’m coming across. Like, am I making sense, did I skip something, are they being polite but lost, that kind of thing. I’ll sometimes over-explain because I’m trying to prevent the confusion, and then I worry I’ve made it worse by adding too much.\n\nSo… yes, self-conscious, definitely. Anxious maybe, but in a situational way, mostly when I know I need to be clear and there are consequences if I’m not.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling more irritable, sad, or euphoric, when you're having trouble explaining your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I have noticed that, actually. And when I’m trying to explain something then, I don’t necessarily feel confused inside — I feel like it’s all very clear, almost too clear, but then it comes out in this flood and other people don’t know where I’m going with it.\n\nBut then if someone interrupts me or says, “I don’t understand,” or even makes a small comment that I’d normally be able to take fine, I can get irritated really quickly. Like sharper than the situation deserves. A collaborator can ask one practical question, and suddenly I feel like they’re blocking the whole vision or doubting me, and I’ll snap or sound defensive. Then later I’ll think, okay, that reaction was much bigger than what they actually said.\n\nSo yes, I think when the explaining gets harder, my mood is often either really elevated, like everything is charged and exciting, or I’m much more irritable than I mean to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself getting easily sidetracked by other thoughts or stimuli when you're trying to explain something?\n\nPatient: Yes, very much. I’ll go from talking about textures, like fabric or concrete or the way light hits something, straight into the cost of materials, and then somehow into what I think the piece is secretly pointing to or what a certain pattern “means.” And when I’m writing it, it doesn’t always feel random to me. It feels like there’s a thread connecting all of it. Yes, there are definitely times when I can be clear. I don’t want to make it sound like every time I open my mouth everything comes out scrambled, because that’s not true. Sometimes it’s really small, almost stupidly small, and then my brain treats it like a doorway into a completely different room.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to focus on one idea for an extended period when you're trying to explain something?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do. Like sharper than the situation deserves. A collaborator can ask one practical question, and suddenly I feel like they’re blocking the whole vision or doubting me, and I’ll snap or sound defensive. Then later I’ll think, okay, that reaction was much bigger than what they actually said.\n\nSo yes, I think when the explaining gets harder, my mood is often either really elevated, like everything is charged and exciting, or I’m much more irritable than I mean to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself getting easily sidetracked by other thoughts or stimuli when you're trying to explain something?\n\nPatient: Yes, very much. Sometimes it’s really small, almost stupidly small, and then my brain treats it like a doorway into a completely different room.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to focus on one idea for an extended period when you're trying to explain something?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do.
